claims.claim: A foreign key is a column (or group of columns) in one table that refers to the primary key of another table.

A foreign key creates a link between two tables: a column that holds a primary key value in one table is referenced by a column in another table, and the linking value is stored on the rows of the referencing table.
The table holding the foreign key is the child (referencing) table; the table holding the referenced primary key is the parent (referenced) table.
A primary key uniquely identifies each row within its own table, whereas a foreign key references the primary key of another table; a foreign key column does not have to be unique.

Referential integrity is the rule that values in the referencing column must match values appearing in some row of the referenced table, so a foreign key value cannot be inserted unless the referenced row exists.
An enforced foreign key also prevents deleting a row in the referenced (parent) table while related rows in the referencing (child) table still point at it.
Because a foreign key stores the referenced row's key rather than a copy of its data, foreign keys let relational databases keep each fact in one place and avoid duplication.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Terminology for the two tables involved in a foreign key reference.
positions: W3Schools calls the table with the foreign key the child table and the table with the primary key the referenced or parent table.
PostgreSQL documentation calls them the referencing table and the referenced table.
Microsoft Learn refers to the foreign key table and the referenced primary key table.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The naming conventions describe the same roles. The lesson leads with referencing/referenced, mentions child/parent as equivalent terms in vocabulary and compare/contrast, and does not present either convention as the only correct one.

sourceRecords.title: SQL FOREIGN KEY Constraint
sourceRecords.notes: Tier B. Read live via curl 2026-08-21. Supports: the working definition of a foreign key as a column in a table that refers to the primary key in another table; the foreign key constraint establishing a link between two tables and preventing actions that would destroy the link; child table vs referenced/parent table naming; enforcement in both directions (no invalid value inserted into the foreign key column, no parent record deleted while related child rows remain); the example of an Orders table storing only PersonID, showing reference instead of duplication. Facts synthesized into original prose; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: SQL PRIMARY KEY Constraint
sourceRecords.notes: Tier B. Read live via curl 2026-08-21. Supports: the primary key constraint uniquely identifying each record in a table, guaranteeing unique values with no NULLs, and allowing only one primary key per table; and the statement that the primary key is the target for foreign key constraints in other tables, which enforces referential integrity between data in two tables. Used for the critical foreign-key-vs-primary-key distinction (uniqueness vs reference). Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.
